Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

vignette: Tavita had been flying commercial routes across the Pacific for two decades when a sudden geopolitical upheaval grounded his aircraft on a remote atoll. During the ensuing unrest, he was seized, blindfolded, and held in a concrete holding cell. For weeks, he endured systematic torture. What frightened him most was the tactical cruelty of his captors: they would drop the room into a heavy, unnatural silence before striking, and they would mock the suffering of fellow detainees, treating moral boundaries as irrelevant. The holding cell smelled of damp earth, old sweat, and rusted iron. When he was finally released and returned to civilian life, the memories did not arrive as flowing narratives. They surfaced as stark, photographic flashes. Whenever he tried to sit with the event, the sheer emotional overwhelm hit him like a physical blow, forcing him to abruptly stop and ground himself. Yet, the moment those photographic memories breached his awareness, his threat monitoring system instantly ignited. He stopped seeing a civilian airport lounge and began scanning for hidden weapons, his eyes darting to every passenger's hands and shoulders, certain that the violence was about to resume. The trauma's architecture quickly reshaped his daily life. As an airline pilot, he knew how to follow checklists, but no procedure could stop the way his brain rewired itself after the cell. The departure gate at the major hub became his new battleground. When passengers pressed close to the boarding barrier, the crowding alone was enough to short-circuit his breathing. When a group of passengers shoved past a spilled coffee, the moral violation of their indifference triggered a visceral surge. That disruption in the crowd did not just annoy him; it pulled the olfactory recall of the holding cell straight into his nose, the phantom scent of rust and antiseptic instantly flooding his system. The sensory trigger directly fueled his threat appraisal, making his pulse hammer and his muscles coil as he watched the shoving match, convinced the next shove would be a tackle to the ground. Weeks turned into months, and his avoidance habits calcified. The unusual silence in his hotel room after the nightly news would instantly tell him that something dangerous was about to happen. This dread drove him to repeatedly check the deadbolt and window latches, even though he had verified them minutes before. His constant threat vigilance, in turn, made him hypersensitive to the slightest change in atmosphere, so that when his wife began to cry over a minor household dispute, the affective expression of her tears immediately acted as a potent trigger. What terrified Tavita was how these loops fed each other. The overwhelming emotional weight of the photographic memories would crash down on him, and the sudden flood of the past would immediately activate his physiological triggers, turning a quiet break into an emergency. Conversely, his amplified threat state lowered his threshold for environmental cues; the moment he felt hunted, his nervous system instantly categorized neutral stimuli-like a crying colleague or a packed gate-as imminent violations of safety. At fifty-three, Tavita sat in his parked SUV outside the clinic, the steering wheel biting into his palms. A recent flight had been the breaking point. During a crosswind landing, the sudden drop in cabin noise triggered a threat appraisal so severe he felt the walls closing in, and he realized his defensive scanning had compromised his situational awareness. His PCL-5 score of 70 reflected the severity, but the lived reality was a tightening circuit. The memories primed his threat system, his threat state magnified his triggers, and those triggers fed the olfactory and photographic intrusions right back into his core. He had come to hope for a way to step out of the loop, terrified that one more trigger would drown him in the past and cost him the cockpit he loved, or worse, the lives of his crew.
